- refine: Transforma um pedido bruto (texto, arquivo de plano ou link — GitHub issue/PR, Jira, Slack) em um plano APROVADO com Contract block, decidindo sozinha se entrevista o usuário, se ilustra outcomes críticos para confirmação e se o risco exige /deep-plan antes da implementação. Substitui o plan mode interativo; usada isoladamente ou como etapa 1 do /implement.

{"body":"Part of #35 (sections 6 + 7; per the maintainer's decision, tooling ships as DOCUMENTED RECIPES, not CLI commands). Pure documentation — the sweep-up sub-issue, two halves that only make sense shipped together.

## Half one: three tools you'll want again, as recipes

- **`build-bitmap-font.py`** — the engine's text path is MonoGame.Extended `BitmapFont`, which means `.spritefont` IS NOT AN OPTION (it yields a `SpriteFont`, a type nothing in the render path accepts) — and today there is **no documented way** from a `.ttf` to a font the engine can render. This tool is that way: rasterise at the face's DESIGN size into the (`.png` + BMFont XML `.fnt`) pair the pipeline already builds, thresholding alpha so a pixel font stays hard-edged instead of antialiased into mush. Scale by whole numbers in game.
- **`frames-to-gif.py`** — raw capture (#52) → GIF, carrying three hard-won rules: nearest-neighbour ONLY when the reduction FACTOR is whole (tested on the factor, not divisibility — 1280→426 at stride 3 is exact, yet a divisibility test wrongly rejects it into blurry area-averaging); ONE shared palette, no dither, or colours crawl between frames; TIME-BASED sampling, or an uneven capture judders the whole clip.
- **`build-sfx.py`** — deterministic sfxr-style synthesis: placeholder-quality audio with a known origin, no third-party terms, byte-identical re-runs. The licensing answer for jams. (The scene-staging pattern that fed the capture pipeline stays game-side; the recipe page points at `gmtk-2026gj`'s `docs/scene-staging.md` for the traps it encodes.)

## Half two: four orphan premises — traps that belong to no single PR, each a real debugging session

1. **DefaultEcs predicate sets re-evaluate only on `Set`**, never on `ref` mutation. Retargeting an entity between render targets by mutating in place leaves it in the OLD draw set while claiming the new target: every field inspects correct, and it renders where nobody is looking. Anything that retargets/re-layers must `entity.Set(...)` after editing. (foundation docs)
2. **Main-target TEXT must set `VisibleComponent` itself.** `CullingSystem` derives bounds from `SpriteInfoComponent`, which text lacks — the failure is an invisible entity with zero errors anywhere. (rendering docs; note the enhancement candidate: make culling text-aware)
3. **A multiply tint cannot whiten.** `SpriteInfoComponent.Color` only darkens; flashing something white needs a runtime-derived white-silhouette texture — and the mask must DETECT straight vs premultiplied alpha, because the same art arrives both ways (the content pipeline premultiplies; a raw file loader does not). Getting it backwards paints an opaque white block over the transparent margin. (rendering docs)
4. **`HierarchySystem` cost scales with ChildOf count** — five passes/frame observed; bake mass-produced children (tiles) unparented, in world space (measured 1.42 → 0.23 ms). Plus the one-way platform pattern: a resolution FILTER (falling AND feet above the top), with the plate's collider dropped by half its thickness so the top face sits flush — centred on the surface line it stands 1px proud and reads as a wall. (collision docs)

## Delivery

- [ ] `docs/recipes/` pages for the three tools, each pointing at `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj` → `tools/` as the reference implementation to adapt
- [ ] Premises entries in foundation / rendering / collision module docs for the four traps, reworded to drop game-provenance lines
- [ ] Cross-link the gif recipe from #52's capture docs

**Value on its own:** four debugging sessions and three rebuilt-from-scratch tools become pages someone reads in five minutes — the cheapest insurance the repo can buy.
","labels":[],"state":"OPEN","title":"docs: tooling recipes (fonts, gif, sfx) + four orphan premises from the shipped game"}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Turn a directory of raw captured frames into a GIF.

The other half of MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT=raw (see docs/scene-staging.md). The game
writes one uncompressed RGBA8888 blob per frame, named so the directory is
self-describing:

    raw_<counter:06>_<width>x<height>_<milliseconds:08>.rgba

and this reads them back, samples them in TIME, scales them, quantises every
frame against ONE palette, and writes an animated GIF.

Three rules are baked in, each of which was a visible artefact before it was:

  * NEAREST-NEIGHBOUR ONLY FOR INTEGER DOWNSCALES. A 3x reduction picks the same
    source pixel in every frame, so the image is stable. A fractional one (say
    1280 -> 480) picks a *different* pixel as the phase drifts, so single-pixel
    details blink in and out between frames and the whole image shimmers. For
    those, area-average instead: every output pixel is a weighted mean of the
    source, so it changes when the picture changes and not otherwise.

  * ONE SHARED PALETTE, NO DITHER. Quantising each frame on its own gives each
    one a palette fitted to that frame, so flat regions creep between slightly
    different colours as the animation runs — the "colour crawl" that makes a
    pixel-art GIF look wet. One palette computed over the whole take fixes every
    colour for the whole take. Dither is off for the same reason: an ordered
    dither pattern that moves is noise that reads as motion.

  * TIME-BASED SAMPLING, NOT INDEX DECIMATION. Taking every Nth file assumes the
    capture was even. It never quite is (a chunk bake, a GC, a window event), so
    decimation turns a hitch into a lasting judder. Instead each output frame
    asks "which captured frame was closest to time T?", which puts the wobble
    back where it belongs: one frame held slightly longer.

Usage
-----
    python3 tools/frames-to-gif.py <frames-dir> -o out.gif
    python3 tools/frames-to-gif.py <frames-dir> -o out.gif --scale 3 --fps 25
    python3 tools/frames-to-gif.py <frames-dir> -o out.gif --width 480 \
        --start 2.0 --duration 8.0 --colors 128

Defaults are chosen for this game: --scale 3 undoes GameplayLayers.CameraZoom
exactly (1280x720 -> 427x240, one output pixel per ART pixel) and is an integer
downscale, so it takes the nearest-neighbour path and stays sharp.

Requires Pillow and numpy (both already used by the other tools here).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import os
import re
import sys

try:
    import numpy as np
    from PIL import Image
except ImportError as exc:  # pragma: no cover - dependency hint
    sys.exit(f"needs Pillow and numpy: {exc}\n  pip3 install pillow numpy")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
build-bitmap-font.py — rasterise a TTF into the (.fnt + .png) pair this project's content pipeline
already builds, so a font drop needs no new importer and no engine change.

    python3 tools/build-bitmap-font.py ~/Downloads/PixelOperator8.ttf --size 8

The pipeline's text path is MonoGame.Extended's BitmapFont (`content.Load<BitmapFont>(...)`), fed by
BitmapFontImporter from a **BMFont XML** descriptor plus a texture page. It does NOT read TTFs, and the
alternative — MonoGame's .spritefont route — produces a SpriteFont, a type nothing in the render path
accepts. Converting up front is therefore both the smaller change and the one that keeps working on the
web head, where the same .fnt goes through the KNI builder untouched.

WHY THE OUTPUT IS THRESHOLDED
FreeType antialiases by default, which is right for a display face and wrong for a pixel font: grey
edge pixels are exactly the "fake pixels" this game's one-pixel-size rule exists to forbid. Every glyph
here is rendered and then thresholded to fully opaque or fully transparent, so the atlas holds hard
pixels. Rasterise at the face's DESIGN size (8 for PixelOperator8) and scale by whole numbers in game;
rasterising at 12 or 20 would reintroduce the blur from the other direction.

    --size N       pixel size to rasterise at (use the face's design size)
    --out-dir      default Gmtk2026.Core/Content/Fonts
    --name         asset base name (default: the TTF's stem)
    --chars        override the character set

The pair is named "<name>.png" + "<name>-fnt.fnt", matching the existing fonts: the "-fnt" suffix keeps
the .fnt's content key distinct from the .png's, since MGCB keys drop the extension.
"""

import argparse
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from xml.sax.saxutils import escape, quoteattr

try:
    from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont
except ImportError:
    sys.exit("Pillow is required: python3 -m pip install Pillow")

content.content:
1	# Recipe — a `.ttf` into a font the engine can render
2	
3	> Rasterise a TrueType face into the (`.png` + BMFont XML `.fnt`) pair the
4	> content pipeline already builds, so a font drop needs no new importer and no
5	> engine change.
6	
7	The engine's text path is MonoGame.Extended's `BitmapFont`. There is no
8	documented route from a `.ttf` to something `DynamicTextComponent.Font` will
9	accept, and the obvious-looking route — MGCB's `.spritefont` — is a dead end.
10	This recipe is the conversion, done once at asset-drop time and committed
11	alongside the art.
12	
13	## Why `.spritefont` is not an option
14	
15	`DynamicTextComponent.Font` is a `MonoGame.Extended.BitmapFonts.BitmapFont`,
16	and `TextPrepSystem` measures and submits glyphs through that path
17	(`rendering-text` premise
18	["Text uses `BitmapFont`, not `SpriteFont`"](../../MonoDreams/rendering-text/docs/premises.md)).
19	MGCB's `.spritefont` route produces a `Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Graphics.SpriteFont`
20	instead — a type **nothing in the render path accepts**. The failure is a
21	compile error at the assignment to `Font`, and there is no cast that fixes it:
22	the two types share no interface and the renderer's measure/draw calls only
23	exist on one of them.
24	
25	The importer on the other side (`BitmapFontImporter`) reads **BMFont
26	descriptors**, not TrueType outlines. So something has to rasterise the face.
27	Doing it up front — a generated `.png` + `.fnt` pair, committed — rather than at
28	build time is both the smaller change and the portable one: the content pipeline
29	stays as shipped, and the same pair is what the web head builds.
30	
31	## What the recipe produces
32	
33	| File | Role | MGCB entry | Content key |
34	|---|---|---|---|
35	| `<name>.png` | the texture page: every glyph shelf-packed, white on transparent | `/importer:TextureImporter` + `/processor:TextureProcessor` | `Fonts/<name>` |
36	| `<name>-fnt.fnt` | BMFont XML descriptor: `<info>` / `<common>` / `<pages>` / `<chars>` | `/importer:BitmapFontImporter` + `/processor:BitmapFontProcessor` | `Fonts/<name>-fnt` |
37	
38	Both are ordinary content entries; both are built. The descriptor's
39	`<pages><page id="0" file="<name>.png"/></pages>` names the page beside it, so
40	the two files must stay in the same content folder and keep the names the
41	generator wrote. Loading is by the **descriptor's** key:
42	
43	```csharp
44	var font = content.Load<BitmapFont>("Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt");
45	```
46	
47	`MonoDreams.Examples.Core/Content/Fonts/` and
48	`MonoDreams.Examples.Core/Content/Content.mgcb` are the working examples — every
49	shipped font in this repo is such a pair.
50	
51	## The `-fnt` suffix is load-bearing, not cosmetic
52	
53	**MGCB content keys drop the extension.** `Fonts/Kaph-Regular.png` and a
54	sibling `Fonts/Kaph-Regular.fnt` would both compile to the key
55	`Fonts/Kaph-Regular` — two assets, one key, one of them silently clobbering the
56	other in the build output. Naming the descriptor `<name>-fnt.fnt` keeps the keys
57	distinct (`Fonts/Kaph-Regular` for the page, `Fonts/Kaph-Regular-fnt` for the
58	font) and is why every font in the repo carries the suffix. Bake it into the
59	generator's output naming; do not leave it to whoever adds the `.mgcb` entry.
60	
61	## Rasterise at the face's design size
62	
63	A pixel face is designed on a grid — 8 px for `PixelOperator8`, 16 for a 16 px
64	face. Rasterise at exactly that size and scale by **whole numbers** in game
65	(`DynamicTextComponent.Scale = 2f`, `3f`, …). Rasterising at 12 or 20 to "get
66	bigger text" resamples a grid-aligned design onto a grid it was not drawn for,
67	which reintroduces the blur from the other direction — the rasteriser invents
68	in-between pixels that the thresholding step then has to guess about.
69	
70	The design size is also what the `.fnt`'s `size`, `lineHeight` and `base` values
71	describe, so a wrong rasterisation size is baked into the metrics as well as the
72	atlas.
73	
74	## Threshold the alpha — and threshold *before* measuring
75	
76	FreeType antialiases by default. That is right for a display face and wrong for
77	a pixel font: grey edge pixels are fake pixels, and they survive every integer
78	upscale as a permanent smear. Render each glyph, then force every pixel to
79	**fully opaque or fully transparent** at an alpha threshold (128 works).
80	
81	Threshold **before** measuring the glyph's ink bounding box. A faint antialiased
82	fringe is a non-zero alpha, so an unthresholded `getbbox()` inflates the box by
83	a pixel on each side — and every `xoffset` / `yoffset` / `width` / `height` in
84	the descriptor inherits the error. The symptom is text that looks a pixel loose
85	in a way no single glyph explains.
86	
87	For a **display face** the inverse applies: keep the antialiasing, rasterise at
88	(or near) the size you will draw, and do not threshold. The recipe is the same
89	script with the threshold pass disabled.
90	
91	## The metrics that are easy to get subtly wrong
92	
93	- **BMFont's `yoffset` is measured down from the top of the line** — which is
94	  exactly what Pillow's `"la"` (left-ascender) anchor does. Draw at the anchor
95	  and the ink bbox *relative to the draw origin* **is** the offset pair. There
96	  is no ascent arithmetic to get wrong, so don't add any.
97	- **`lineHeight = ascent + descent` and `base = ascent`**, taken from the face's
98	  own metrics rather than measured off the atlas.
99	- **A one-pixel transparent gutter between packed glyphs.** Without it a
100	  neighbour's edge column can bleed into a sampled glyph edge under any
101	  filtering.
102	- **A character the face lacks must be reported, not shipped.** Rasterise a
103	  private-use codepoint (U+E000 — no real face maps it) to get the face's
104	  `.notdef` bitmap, then compare every requested character's mask against it and
105	  skip + print the matches. Otherwise the atlas quietly ships tofu boxes that
106	  only surface on screen, in a string nobody tested.
107	
108	## The web head takes the same pair
109	
110	There is no per-platform font source. Content is built **per platform** (a
111	desktop `.xnb` is not a BlazorGL one), but the web build runs KNI's MGCB over
112	the same `.fnt` + `.png` with the same importer/processor pair — the asset is
113	untouched. On macOS/Linux the KNI content build needs the native-lib shim,
114	including staging `KNI.Extended.Content.Pipeline.dll` so the BitmapFont
115	importer's dependency probe resolves; see
116	[`docs/web-targeting.md`](../web-targeting.md) § "macOS / Linux native-lib shim".
117	
118	## Usage sketch
119	
120	```bash
121	python3 -m pip install Pillow
122	
123	# Rasterise at the face's design size, straight into the game's content tree.
124	python3 tools/build-bitmap-font.py ~/Downloads/PixelOperator8.ttf \
125	    --size 8 --out-dir MyGame.Core/Content/Fonts
126	# PixelOperator8: N glyph(s) at 8px -> WxH page, lineHeight L, base B
127	#   MyGame.Core/Content/Fonts/PixelOperator8.png
128	#   MyGame.Core/Content/Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt.fnt
129	#   content keys: Fonts/PixelOperator8  and  Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt
130	```
131	
132	Then add both to `Content.mgcb` (copy an existing font's two blocks — the page
133	uses `TextureImporter`/`TextureProcessor`, the descriptor
134	`BitmapFontImporter`/`BitmapFontProcessor`) and use it like any other font:
135	
136	```csharp
137	var font = content.Load<BitmapFont>("Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt");
138	
139	entity.Set(new DynamicTextComponent
140	{
141	    Font = font,
142	    TextContent = "READY",
143	    Color = Color.White,
144	    Scale = 3f,                 // whole numbers only for a pixel face
145	    Target = RenderTargetID.HUD,
146	});
147	```
148	
149	**Dependencies:** Pillow (`python3 -m pip install Pillow`). Nothing else.
150	
151	## Adapt these
152	
153	The reference script is written for one game. When you copy it:
154	
155	- **`--out-dir` default** — it defaults to that game's own
156	  `Gmtk2026.Core/Content/Fonts`. Point it at your content tree.
157	- **The character set** (`DEFAULT_CHARS`) — printable ASCII plus the handful of
158	  marks that game's strings use (`—–·×…°`). Add whatever yours needs; an absent
159	  character is skipped and reported, not substituted.
160	- **`ALPHA_THRESHOLD` (128), and whether to threshold at all** — drop the pass
161	  for a display face.
162	- **`ATLAS_MAX_WIDTH` (512) and `GLYPH_PAD` (1)** — a large face over a wide
163	  character set wants a bigger page.
164	- **The `-fnt` suffix** — keep it. It is the part of the naming that the content
165	  pipeline actually constrains.
166	
167	## Reference implementation
168	
169	[`tools/build-bitmap-font.py`](https://github.com/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj/blob/main/tools/build-bitmap-font.py)
170	in `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj`.
171	
172	This is the implementation to **copy and adapt**, not a dependency to install.
173	The engine deliberately does not vendor the script: tooling of this shape ships
174	as a documented recipe, so each game owns a version tuned to its own content
175	tree, character set and face — the same ownership model as the modules
176	themselves. What to change is listed under "Adapt these" above.

# Recipe — a `.ttf` into a font the engine can render

> Rasterise a TrueType face into the (`.png` + BMFont XML `.fnt`) pair the
> content pipeline already builds, so a font drop needs no new importer and no
> engine change.

The engine's text path is MonoGame.Extended's `BitmapFont`. There is no
documented route from a `.ttf` to something `DynamicTextComponent.Font` will
accept, and the obvious-looking route — MGCB's `.spritefont` — is a dead end.
This recipe is the conversion, done once at asset-drop time and committed
alongside the art.

## Why `.spritefont` is not an option

`DynamicTextComponent.Font` is a `MonoGame.Extended.BitmapFonts.BitmapFont`,
and `TextPrepSystem` measures and submits glyphs through that path
(`rendering-text` premise
["Text uses `BitmapFont`, not `SpriteFont`"](../../MonoDreams/rendering-text/docs/premises.md)).
MGCB's `.spritefont` route produces a `Microsoft.Xna.Framework.Graphics.SpriteFont`
instead — a type **nothing in the render path accepts**. The failure is a
compile error at the assignment to `Font`, and there is no cast that fixes it:
the two types share no interface and the renderer's measure/draw calls only
exist on one of them.

The importer on the other side (`BitmapFontImporter`) reads **BMFont
descriptors**, not TrueType outlines. So something has to rasterise the face.
Doing it up front — a generated `.png` + `.fnt` pair, committed — rather than at
build time is both the smaller change and the portable one: the content pipeline
stays as shipped, and the same pair is what the web head builds.

## What the recipe produces

| File | Role | MGCB entry | Content key |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<name>.png` | the texture page: every glyph shelf-packed, white on transparent | `/importer:TextureImporter` + `/processor:TextureProcessor` | `Fonts/<name>` |
| `<name>-fnt.fnt` | BMFont XML descriptor: `<info>` / `<common>` / `<pages>` / `<chars>` | `/importer:BitmapFontImporter` + `/processor:BitmapFontProcessor` | `Fonts/<name>-fnt` |

Both are ordinary content entries; both are built. The descriptor's
`<pages><page id="0" file="<name>.png"/></pages>` names the page beside it, so
the two files must stay in the same content folder and keep the names the
generator wrote. Loading is by the **descriptor's** key:

```csharp
var font = content.Load<BitmapFont>("Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt");
```

`MonoDreams.Examples.Core/Content/Fonts/` and
`MonoDreams.Examples.Core/Content/Content.mgcb` are the working examples — every
shipped font in this repo is such a pair.

## The `-fnt` suffix is load-bearing, not cosmetic

**MGCB content keys drop the extension.** `Fonts/Kaph-Regular.png` and a
sibling `Fonts/Kaph-Regular.fnt` would both compile to the key
`Fonts/Kaph-Regular` — two assets, one key, one of them silently clobbering the
other in the build output. Naming the descriptor `<name>-fnt.fnt` keeps the keys
distinct (`Fonts/Kaph-Regular` for the page, `Fonts/Kaph-Regular-fnt` for the
font) and is why every font in the repo carries the suffix. Bake it into the
generator's output naming; do not leave it to whoever adds the `.mgcb` entry.

## Rasterise at the face's design size

A pixel face is designed on a grid — 8 px for `PixelOperator8`, 16 for a 16 px
face. Rasterise at exactly that size and scale by **whole numbers** in game
(`DynamicTextComponent.Scale = 2f`, `3f`, …). Rasterising at 12 or 20 to "get
bigger text" resamples a grid-aligned design onto a grid it was not drawn for,
which reintroduces the blur from the other direction — the rasteriser invents
in-between pixels that the thresholding step then has to guess about.

The design size is also what the `.fnt`'s `size`, `lineHeight` and `base` values
describe, so a wrong rasterisation size is baked into the metrics as well as the
atlas.

## Threshold the alpha — and threshold *before* measuring

FreeType antialiases by default. That is right for a display face and wrong for
a pixel font: grey edge pixels are fake pixels, and they survive every integer
upscale as a permanent smear. Render each glyph, then force every pixel to
**fully opaque or fully transparent** at an alpha threshold (128 works).

Threshold **before** measuring the glyph's ink bounding box. A faint antialiased
fringe is a non-zero alpha, so an unthresholded `getbbox()` inflates the box by
a pixel on each side — and every `xoffset` / `yoffset` / `width` / `height` in
the descriptor inherits the error. The symptom is text that looks a pixel loose
in a way no single glyph explains.

For a **display face** the inverse applies: keep the antialiasing, rasterise at
(or near) the size you will draw, and do not threshold. The recipe is the same
script with the threshold pass disabled.

## The metrics that are easy to get subtly wrong

- **BMFont's `yoffset` is measured down from the top of the line** — which is
  exactly what Pillow's `"la"` (left-ascender) anchor does. Draw at the anchor
  and the ink bbox *relative to the draw origin* **is** the offset pair. There
  is no ascent arithmetic to get wrong, so don't add any.
- **`lineHeight = ascent + descent` and `base = ascent`**, taken from the face's
  own metrics rather than measured off the atlas.
- **A one-pixel transparent gutter between packed glyphs.** Without it a
  neighbour's edge column can bleed into a sampled glyph edge under any
  filtering.
- **A character the face lacks must be reported, not shipped.** Rasterise a
  private-use codepoint (U+E000 — no real face maps it) to get the face's
  `.notdef` bitmap, then compare every requested character's mask against it and
  skip + print the matches. Otherwise the atlas quietly ships tofu boxes that
  only surface on screen, in a string nobody tested.

## The web head takes the same pair

There is no per-platform font source. Content is built **per platform** (a
desktop `.xnb` is not a BlazorGL one), but the web build runs KNI's MGCB over
the same `.fnt` + `.png` with the same importer/processor pair — the asset is
untouched. On macOS/Linux the KNI content build needs the native-lib shim,
including staging `KNI.Extended.Content.Pipeline.dll` so the BitmapFont
importer's dependency probe resolves; see
[`docs/web-targeting.md`](../web-targeting.md) § "macOS / Linux native-lib shim".

## Usage sketch

```bash
python3 -m pip install Pillow

# Rasterise at the face's design size, straight into the game's content tree.
python3 tools/build-bitmap-font.py ~/Downloads/PixelOperator8.ttf \
    --size 8 --out-dir MyGame.Core/Content/Fonts
# PixelOperator8: N glyph(s) at 8px -> WxH page, lineHeight L, base B
#   MyGame.Core/Content/Fonts/PixelOperator8.png
#   MyGame.Core/Content/Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt.fnt
#   content keys: Fonts/PixelOperator8  and  Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt
```

Then add both to `Content.mgcb` (copy an existing font's two blocks — the page
uses `TextureImporter`/`TextureProcessor`, the descriptor
`BitmapFontImporter`/`BitmapFontProcessor`) and use it like any other font:

```csharp
var font = content.Load<BitmapFont>("Fonts/PixelOperator8-fnt");

entity.Set(new DynamicTextComponent
{
    Font = font,
    TextContent = "READY",
    Color = Color.White,
    Scale = 3f,                 // whole numbers only for a pixel face
    Target = RenderTargetID.HUD,
});
```

**Dependencies:** Pillow (`python3 -m pip install Pillow`). Nothing else.

## Adapt these

The reference script is written for one game. When you copy it:

- **`--out-dir` default** — it defaults to that game's own
  `Gmtk2026.Core/Content/Fonts`. Point it at your content tree.
- **The character set** (`DEFAULT_CHARS`) — printable ASCII plus the handful of
  marks that game's strings use (`—–·×…°`). Add whatever yours needs; an absent
  character is skipped and reported, not substituted.
- **`ALPHA_THRESHOLD` (128), and whether to threshold at all** — drop the pass
  for a display face.
- **`ATLAS_MAX_WIDTH` (512) and `GLYPH_PAD` (1)** — a large face over a wide
  character set wants a bigger page.
- **The `-fnt` suffix** — keep it. It is the part of the naming that the content
  pipeline actually constrains.

## Reference implementation

[`tools/build-bitmap-font.py`](https://github.com/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj/blob/main/tools/build-bitmap-font.py)
in `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj`.

This is the implementation to **copy and adapt**, not a dependency to install.
The engine deliberately does not vendor the script: tooling of this shape ships
as a documented recipe, so each game owns a version tuned to its own content
tree, character set and face — the same ownership model as the modules
themselves. What to change is listed under "Adapt these" above.

1	# Recipe — raw captured frames into an animated GIF
2	
3	> The other half of `MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT=raw`. The engine writes exact pixels
4	> at full frame rate; assembling them into a shareable clip is a tooling job
5	> that lives outside the frame loop.
6	
7	`ScreenshotCaptureSystem` in the [`debug`](../../MonoDreams/debug/docs/overview.md)
8	module has a raw mode (`CaptureFormat.Raw`) that dumps one uncompressed
9	RGBA8888 blob per frame, synchronously, allocating nothing per frame — so the
10	recording is of the game the player would have played rather than of a game
11	crawling behind a PNG encoder. **The engine ships no mp4/gif writer, and that is
12	a boundary rather than a gap:** an encoder inside the capture path would put a
13	codec's timing behaviour inside the loop being verified. This recipe is the
14	outside-the-loop half.
15	
16	Read the [`debug` overview § Frame capture](../../MonoDreams/debug/docs/overview.md#frame-capture)
17	first for the env contract and the disk-cost table. Raw capture is a firehose —
18	~3.5 MiB per frame at 1280x720, ~220 MB/s at 60 fps — so
19	`MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_MAX_FRAMES` is a safety valve, not decoration.
20	
21	## The filename contract
22	
23	Raw frames are named so the directory is self-describing and needs no manifest
24	that could fall out of step with it. Verified against
25	`MonoDreams/debug/System/ScreenshotCaptureSystem.cs`:
26	
27	```
28	raw_{counter:D6}_{width}x{height}_{gametimeMs:D8}.rgba
29	```
30	
31	| Field | Meaning |
32	|---|---|
33	| `counter` | zero-based, six digits, zero-padded. Incremented **only after a successful write**, so the sequence is contiguous — a gap means frames were lost, not merely renamed. |
34	| `width`x`height` | the backbuffer geometry of *that* frame. It can change mid-run if the window is resized. |
35	| `gametimeMs` | total game time as an **integer millisecond count**, eight digits, zero-padded (`(int)MathF.Round(gameTime * 1000f)`). Integer rather than a formatted float on purpose: a decimal separator is culture-dependent and would make any indexing tool machine-specific. |
36	| contents | exactly `width * height * 4` bytes, RGBA8888, no header. |
37	
38	The reference tool parses this with `^raw_(\d+)_(\d+)x(\d+)_(\d+)\.rgba$` and
39	sorts by `(millis, counter)`. **That regex matches what MonoDreams writes
40	today** — no adaptation needed. If a future engine change alters the name, the
41	regex (`FRAME_RE`) is the single place to follow it, and the byte-length check in
42	the loader is what will otherwise fail first.
43	
44	Two refusals in the tool are worth keeping when you copy it:
45	
46	- **One geometry per directory, or refuse.** Mixed sizes mean the window was
47	  resized mid-capture — two takes in one folder. Silently stretching the shorter
48	  one is a worse answer than saying so.
49	- **A frame whose byte length isn't `w * h * 4` is a truncated write**, i.e. the
50	  capture was killed mid-write. Say which file and stop; delete the last frame
51	  and retry.
52	
53	## Three rules, each of which was a visible artefact first
54	
55	### 1. Nearest-neighbour only when the reduction **factor** is whole
56	
57	A whole factor picks the same source pixel in every frame, so the image is rock
58	stable: a stride of 3 samples columns 0, 3, 6, … in every frame of the take. A
59	**fractional** factor (1280 → 480, say) picks a *different* source pixel as the
60	phase drifts, so single-pixel details blink in and out between frames and the
61	whole image shimmers. Area-average those instead (Pillow's `BOX`): every output
62	pixel is a weighted mean of the source box, so it changes when the picture
63	changes and not otherwise.
64	
65	**Test the factor, not divisibility of the dimensions.** This is the part that is
66	easy to get wrong and expensive to notice. 1280 / 3 = 426.67, so 1280 is not a
67	multiple of any 3x output width — a `width % out_w == 0` test therefore *rejects*
68	a 3x reduction and sends it down the area-average path, softening every pixel of
69	art the reduction existed to preserve. But a stride of 3 over 1280 columns picks
70	0, 3, 6, …, 1278 — **427 columns**, and exactly the nearest-neighbour reduction
71	that was wanted.
72	
73	What the reference tool actually does (`plan_scale`) is the correct form: it
74	computes `factor = width / out_width` (or takes `--scale` directly) and takes the
75	strided path when
76	
77	```python
78	factor >= 1.0 and abs(factor - round(factor)) < 1e-9
79	```
80	
81	— a whole-factor test, with the output size derived by **ceil division**
82	(`-(-width // stride)` → 427, not 426). Its module docstring calls this "integer
83	downscales", which is loose wording for the same thing; the code and its
84	`plan_scale` docstring are the authority, and they test the factor. Symptom when
85	this is wrong: the GIF looks slightly out of focus and is roughly a third larger,
86	because blurring invents colours the palette then has to spend entries on.
87	
88	### 2. One shared palette over the whole take, no dither
89	
90	Quantising each frame on its own fits each frame its own palette, so flat regions
91	creep between slightly different colours as the animation runs — the "colour
92	crawl" that makes a pixel-art GIF look wet. Fit **one** palette over the whole
93	take and map every frame against it.
94	
95	Fit it over a *spread* of frames, not the first one: a take that opens in a dark
96	room and ends in lava needs both colour populations, and a palette fitted to
97	frame 0 bands the second half. The reference tool stacks ~24 evenly-spaced frames
98	into one tall image so median cut sees them as a single colour population.
99	
100	**Dither off**, for the same reason as rule 1: an ordered dither pattern that
101	moves between frames is noise that reads as motion.
102	
103	### 3. Time-based sampling, not index decimation
104	
105	Taking every Nth file assumes the capture was even. It never quite is — a GC, a
106	chunk bake, a window event — so decimation turns one hitch into a lasting
107	judder: every frame after the hitch is picked from the wrong moment. Instead, for
108	each output instant T, pick **the captured frame whose embedded game time is
109	closest to T**. That puts the wobble back where it belongs: one frame held
110	slightly longer, and everything after it back on time.
111	
112	Because the captures are sorted and the wanted times only move forward, this is a
113	single walk over the list, not a scan per output frame.
114	
115	**A GIF aside that belongs with the sampling:** GIF stores frame delays in
116	hundredths of a second, so only frame rates dividing 100 land on an exact delay —
117	**50 / 25 / 20 / 10**. Anything else is silently rounded by every viewer, which
118	makes playback speed subtly wrong and impossible to debug from the file. Say so
119	rather than rounding quietly.
120	
121	## Usage sketch
122	
123	```bash
124	python3 -m pip install pillow numpy
125	
126	SCRATCH=/tmp/take
127	mkdir -p "$SCRATCH"
128	
129	# 1. Capture. Release build, so the frame budget is the game's and not the
130	#    debugger's. Always cap the frame count — 600 frames is ten seconds.
131	MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR="$SCRATCH" \
132	MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT=raw \
133	MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_MAX_FRAMES=600 \
134	dotnet run --project MyGame.Desktop -c Release
135	
136	# 2. Assemble. --scale is the reduction FACTOR; keep it whole to stay sharp.
137	python3 tools/frames-to-gif.py "$SCRATCH" -o take.gif --fps 25 --scale 3
138	# 600 frames, 1280x720, 10.02s captured (59.8 fps average)
139	# 251 output frames at 427x240, nearest-neighbour (exact 1/3 reduction)
140	
141	# 3. Delete the frames. They are gigabytes.
142	rm -f "$SCRATCH"/*.rgba
143	```
144	
145	Useful options in the reference tool: `--width N` (output width, overrides
146	`--scale`), `--start S` / `--duration S` (trim the take in seconds of capture
147	time), `--colors N` (palette size, 2..256), `--palette-samples N` (frames the
148	shared palette is fitted over).
149	
150	**Dependencies:** Pillow and numpy (`python3 -m pip install pillow numpy`).
151	
152	## Staging the scene you want to film
153	
154	Capturing is the easy half; getting the game into the situation worth filming on
155	the first frame is the other one. That pattern — an env-selected staging system
156	that arms a named scene a few frames into boot, so a take needs no twenty minutes
157	of play first — stays **game-side**: it manipulates game-specific items, bosses
158	and world generation, so it is not an engine primitive. What generalises is the
159	list of traps, and the reference repo's
160	[`docs/scene-staging.md`](https://github.com/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj/blob/main/docs/scene-staging.md)
161	encodes them: stage *after* the world is built (spawners and deferred props run a
162	frame or more late), write authored inputs rather than derived maxima (a system
163	that reconciles a maximum every frame overwrites a poked one before it is drawn),
164	suppress any cinematic that takes the camera, keep the subject inside the ranges
165	the game's own systems gate on, and treat a mistyped scene name as an error that
166	stages nothing rather than a silent fallback.
167	
168	Read it before building your own staging harness; it is the accumulated cost of
169	doing this without one.
170	
171	## Adapt these
172	
173	- **`--scale` default (3)** — in the reference game a 3x reduction exactly undoes
174	  its camera zoom, giving one output pixel per *art* pixel. Set yours to your own
175	  zoom, or pass `--width`.
176	- **`--fps` default (25)** and the `EXACT_FPS` set — keep the exactness check;
177	  change the default if your takes are slower or faster.
178	- **`--colors` (192) and `--palette-samples` (24)** — a take with two very
179	  different lighting regimes wants more samples; a flat one wants fewer colours
180	  and a smaller file.
181	- **`FRAME_RE`** — only if a future engine version changes the raw filename
182	  format. It matches today's.
183	- **Output paths** — the reference tool writes wherever `-o` says and reads
184	  wherever the capture landed; nothing game-specific there.
185	
186	## Reference implementation
187	
188	[`tools/frames-to-gif.py`](https://github.com/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj/blob/main/tools/frames-to-gif.py)
189	in `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj`.
190	
191	This is the implementation to **copy and adapt**, not a dependency to install.
192	The engine deliberately does not vendor the script — assembling a clip is a
193	tooling concern that must stay outside the capture path being verified, and each
194	game's zoom, palette and take length differ. What to change is listed under
195	"Adapt these" above.

whole image shimmers. Area-average those instead (Pillow's `BOX`): every output
pixel is a weighted mean of the source box, so it changes when the picture
changes and not otherwise.

**Test the factor, not divisibility of the dimensions.** This is the part that is
easy to get wrong and expensive to notice. 1280 / 3 = 426.67, so 1280 is not a
multiple of any 3x output width — a `width % out_w == 0` test therefore *rejects*
a 3x reduction and sends it down the area-average path, softening every pixel of
art the reduction existed to preserve. But a stride of 3 over 1280 columns picks
0, 3, 6, …, 1278 — **427 columns**, and exactly the nearest-neighbour reduction
that was wanted.

What the reference tool actually does (`plan_scale`) is the correct form: it
computes `factor = width / out_width` (or takes `--scale` directly) and takes the
strided path when

```python
factor >= 1.0 and abs(factor - round(factor)) < 1e-9
```

— a whole-factor test, with the output size derived by **ceil division**
(`-(-width // stride)` → 427, not 426). Its module docstring calls this "integer
downscales", which is loose wording for the same thing; the code and its
`plan_scale` docstring are the authority, and they test the factor. Symptom when
this is wrong: the GIF looks slightly out of focus and is roughly a third larger,
because blurring invents colours the palette then has to spend entries on.

### 2. One shared palette over the whole take, no dither

Quantising each frame on its own fits each frame its own palette, so flat regions
creep between slightly different colours as the animation runs — the "colour
crawl" that makes a pixel-art GIF look wet. Fit **one** palette over the whole
take and map every frame against it.

Fit it over a *spread* of frames, not the first one: a take that opens in a dark
room and ends in lava needs both colour populations, and a palette fitted to
frame 0 bands the second half. The reference tool stacks ~24 evenly-spaced frames
into one tall image so median cut sees them as a single colour population.

**Dither off**, for the same reason as rule 1: an ordered dither pattern that
moves between frames is noise that reads as motion.

### 3. Time-based sampling, not index decimation

Taking every Nth file assumes the capture was even. It never quite is — a GC, a
chunk bake, a window event — so decimation turns one hitch into a lasting
judder: every frame after the hitch is picked from the wrong moment. Instead, for
each output instant T, pick **the captured frame whose embedded game time is
closest to T**. That puts the wobble back where it belongs: one frame held
slightly longer, and everything after it back on time.

Because the captures are sorted and the wanted times only move forward, this is a
single walk over the list, not a scan per output frame.

**A GIF aside that belongs with the sampling:** GIF stores frame delays in
hundredths of a second, so only frame rates dividing 100 land on an exact delay —
**50 / 25 / 20 / 10**. Anything else is silently rounded by every viewer, which
makes playback speed subtly wrong and impossible to debug from the file. Say so
rather than rounding quietly.

## Usage sketch

```bash
python3 -m pip install pillow numpy

SCRATCH=/tmp/take
mkdir -p "$SCRATCH"

# 1. Capture. Release build, so the frame budget is the game's and not the
#    debugger's. Always cap the frame count — 600 frames is ten seconds.
MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR="$SCRATCH" \
MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT=raw \
MONODREAMS_SCREENSHOT_MAX_FRAMES=600 \
dotnet run --project MyGame.Desktop -c Release

# 2. Assemble. --scale is the reduction FACTOR; keep it whole to stay sharp.
python3 tools/frames-to-gif.py "$SCRATCH" -o take.gif --fps 25 --scale 3
# 600 frames, 1280x720, 10.02s captured (59.8 fps average)
# 251 output frames at 427x240, nearest-neighbour (exact 1/3 reduction)

# 3. Delete the frames. They are gigabytes.
rm -f "$SCRATCH"/*.rgba
```

Useful options in the reference tool: `--width N` (output width, overrides
`--scale`), `--start S` / `--duration S` (trim the take in seconds of capture
time), `--colors N` (palette size, 2..256), `--palette-samples N` (frames the
shared palette is fitted over).

**Dependencies:** Pillow and numpy (`python3 -m pip install pillow numpy`).

## Staging the scene you want to film

Capturing is the easy half; getting the game into the situation worth filming on
the first frame is the other one. That pattern — an env-selected staging system
that arms a named scene a few frames into boot, so a take needs no twenty minutes
of play first — stays **game-side**: it manipulates game-specific items, bosses
and world generation, so it is not an engine primitive. What generalises is the
list of traps, and the reference repo's
[`docs/scene-staging.md`](https://github.com/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj/blob/main/docs/scene-staging.md)
encodes them: stage *after* the world is built (spawners and deferred props run a
frame or more late), write authored inputs rather than derived maxima (a system
that reconciles a maximum every frame overwrites a poked one before it is drawn),
suppress any cinematic that takes the camera, keep the subject inside the ranges
the game's own systems gate on, and treat a mistyped scene name as an error that
stages nothing rather than a silent fallback.

Read it before building your own staging harness; it is the accumulated cost of
doing this without one.

## Adapt these

- **`--scale` default (3)** — in the reference game a 3x reduction exactly undoes
  its camera zoom, giving one output pixel per *art* pixel. Set yours to your own
  zoom, or pass `--width`.
- **`--fps` default (25)** and the `EXACT_FPS` set — keep the exactness check;
  change the default if your takes are slower or faster.
- **`--colors` (192) and `--palette-samples` (24)** — a take with two very
  different lighting regimes wants more samples; a flat one wants fewer colours
  and a smaller file.
- **`FRAME_RE`** — only if a future engine version changes the raw filename
  format. It matches today's.
- **Output paths** — the reference tool writes wherever `-o` says and reads
  wherever the capture landed; nothing game-specific there.

## Reference implementation

[`tools/frames-to-gif.py`](https://github.com/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj/blob/main/tools/frames-to-gif.py)
in `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj`.

This is the implementation to **copy and adapt**, not a dependency to install.
The engine deliberately does not vendor the script — assembling a clip is a
tooling concern that must stay outside the capture path being verified, and each
game's zoom, palette and take length differ. What to change is listed under
"Adapt these" above.

# Recipe — deterministic sfxr-style sound effects

> Synthesise a game's sound effects as short 16-bit mono WAVs from a script, so
> the origin is known, the licence question never arises, and re-running the
> script produces byte-identical files.

Placeholder audio has a sourcing problem, not a quality problem. "Only free
sounds, and I need to know the origin so I can credit it" is a constraint that
costs hours per sound to satisfy from asset packs, and third-party terms can
change after shipping. Generating the sounds answers it completely and
permanently: **the origin is the script**, there is nothing to attribute, and no
external terms exist to change. It also makes every sound *tweakable* — if the
coin is too bright, edit a number and re-run, which is not true of a downloaded
clip.

The output is placeholder-grade by design. Licensed or recorded material sounds
richer and is the right end state for the sounds that matter; this recipe is how
you get a complete, credited soundscape on day one of a jam and replace it
selectively later.

## The mechanism

The synthesis is deliberately **sfxr-shaped** — the palette a pixel-art game
wants — and small enough to read in one sitting:

- **Short envelopes over square / triangle / sine / noise, with pitch sweeps.** A
  rising sweep reads as gain, a falling one as impact. Filtered noise with a
  moving cutoff reads as a *material* (wood, cloth, stone) rather than as static.
- **A per-sound recipe is a function** `fn(i, n) -> [-1, 1]`, composed from
  primitives (`tone_sweep`, `noise_burst`, `sine`, `mix`) and rendered by one
  `render(name, seconds, fn, volume)` helper that applies the shared envelope,
  clips, and writes the WAV.
- **Nothing longer than ~0.3 s.** These play constantly; length is what turns a
  sound effect into an irritation.
- **16-bit mono at 22050 Hz.** Plenty for short blips and a quarter the size of
  44.1 kHz stereo — which matters here, because the audio module holds
  everything in RAM as `SoundEffect` (see below).

**Determinism is the load-bearing property.** The noise generator is a tiny LCG
**seeded per sound**, so "noise" is reproducible across runs and machines: two
runs produce byte-identical WAVs and the repo sees no churn. Nothing reads the
clock, `random` without a seed, or the filesystem. That is what makes the files
safe to commit and the script safe to re-run.

**One guard worth copying: a do-not-overwrite list.** Once a synthesised
placeholder has been replaced by a licensed or recorded clip, re-running the
script would overwrite audio that cost money and a licence to obtain, replace it
with a beep, and **report success**. The reference tool keeps a `LICENSED` set of
names that `render` refuses, printing why and pointing at the attribution file
that records the replacement. Add a name to that set the moment you replace a
sound.

**No dependencies.** The reference script uses only the Python standard library
(`math`, `struct`, `wave`) — unlike the other recipes here, there is no Pillow or
numpy to install.

## Feeding the engine

The output is plain `.wav`, which is exactly what the
[`audio`](../../MonoDreams/audio/docs/overview.md) module consumes. The module is
`SoundEffect`-only — one XNA API that behaves identically on MonoGame DesktopGL
and KNI/BlazorGL — and reaches it through `ContentAudioPlayer`, the default
`IAudioPlayer` backed by `ContentManager.Load<SoundEffect>` and cached per key.

1. **Add each WAV to `Content.mgcb`** with the sound-effect importer/processor:

   ```
   #begin Sounds/hit.wav
   /importer:WavImporter
   /processor:SoundEffectProcessor
   /processorParam:Quality=Best
   /build:Sounds/hit.wav
   ```

2. **The content key is the sound key.** `Sounds/hit.wav` → `Sounds/hit`, which
   is what you pass the module:

   ```csharp
   // one-shot, fire and forget
   world.Publish(new PlaySoundRequest("Sounds/hit", 0.6f));

   // entity-owned playback with a lifecycle (loops, interruptible sources)
   entity.Set(new AudioSourceComponent("Sounds/wind", loop: true, volume: 0.3f));
   ```

3. **Register `AudioSystem`, or the game is silently mute** — every
   `PlaySoundRequest` publishes into a world with no listener and every
   `AudioSourceComponent` sits inert, with no exception and no log line:

   ```csharp
   var audioPlayer = new ContentAudioPlayer(content);
   pipeline.Add(new AudioSystem(world, audioPlayer));
   ```

4. **Warm the cache from a loading moment** —
   `audioPlayer.Preload(new[] { "Sounds/hit", "Sounds/coin", … })` — so no first
   `Play` pays the disk read + PCM decode mid-frame. An unwarmed game hitches once
   per distinct sound, which reads as a gameplay bug.

Two module facts that shape the recipe: everything (music included) is held in
RAM as `SoundEffect` — roughly 10 MB per minute of 44.1 kHz stereo — so short
22 kHz mono blips are the cheap case and long tracks are a known limitation; and
in edit-capable screens `AudioSystem` is registered `EditTimeBehavior.Freeze`,
since audio is game logic. See the module's
[premises](../../MonoDreams/audio/docs/premises.md) for the full contracts.

**On the web head**, a `.wav` in the `.mgcb` means the KNI content build shells
out to `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe`, which the KNI builder package does not ship for any
OS — the build fails with `Failed to open file <name> … not DRM protected` until
they are staged. See
[`docs/web-targeting.md`](../web-targeting.md) § "macOS / Linux native-lib shim",
step 5.

## Usage sketch

```bash
# No dependencies — stdlib only.
python3 tools/build-sfx.py
# writing MyGame.Core/Content/Sounds
#   coin.wav  120ms
#   hit.wav   100ms
#   land.wav   80ms
#   chest.wav  SKIPPED — a licensed clip owns this sound (see Content/ATTRIBUTION.md)
# done — add each to Content.mgcb (SoundEffect)
```

Editing a sound is editing one line in the script and re-running:

```python
# The hit: a hard, falling crack. Noise for the impact, a dropping square
# for the weight.
render("hit", 0.10, mix(noise_burst(23, tilt=0.5), tone_sweep(440, 150, 0.5)),
       volume=0.30)
```

Re-run, listen, adjust. Because the noise seed is fixed, the only thing that
changed between two runs is the number you edited.

## Adapt these

- **The output directory** — the reference tool hardcodes that game's
  `Gmtk2026.Core/Content/Sounds` relative to the repo root. Point it at your
  content tree.
- **The sound list itself** — the recipes in `main()` are that game's vocabulary
  (`coin`, `chest`, `swing`, `hit`, `hurt`, `land`, `enemy-death`). Keep the
  primitives, replace the list. The names become your content keys.
- **The `LICENSED` set** — starts empty for a new game; add a name the moment a
  real clip replaces a placeholder, and record the replacement wherever you keep
  attribution.
- **`RATE` (22050) and the per-sound `volume`s** — mixing levels are per-game;
  the quietest sound should be the one that plays most often.
- **The noise seeds** — any fixed integers work. What matters is that they are
  fixed.

## Reference implementation

[`tools/build-sfx.py`](https://github.com/roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj/blob/main/tools/build-sfx.py)
in `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj`.

This is the implementation to **copy and adapt**, not a dependency to install.
The engine deliberately does not vendor the script: a game's sound vocabulary,
mixing levels and content layout are game-specific, so tooling of this shape
ships as a documented recipe that each game owns a tuned copy of. What to change
is listed under "Adapt these" above.

+## A `ChildOf`-parented collider costs hierarchy work every frame; mass-produced statics go unparented
+
+Parent a collider when it must ride a body or share its lifecycle — `ColliderBody.Resolve`
+walks the `ChildOf` chain, so that link IS the model. A collider with no physics ancestor is
+already its own body (static geometry, trigger zones), so parenting it buys nothing but cost,
+and the cost is per parented entity per frame: `HierarchySystem.Update` makes **three full
+passes over the `ChildOf` set** every frame — `DisposeOrphans`, then
+`EntityHierarchy.Rebuild` (which also clears and repopulates two dictionaries, allocating a
+`List<Entity>` per parent), then `SyncTransformParents` — on top of the **three passes over
+the `TransformComponent` set** in `PropagateDirtyFlags` (build the parent→children map,
+collect the changed roots, clear every propagation flag). A parented collider is therefore
+visited six times a frame plus a dictionary insert; an unparented one, three. That is fine for
+a handful and dominant for thousands: when a view's worth of mass-produced tile children
+stopped being parented, the measured hierarchy cost fell from **1.42 ms to 0.23 ms per
+frame**. So a producer that mass-produces static colliders should spawn them UNPARENTED with
+their pose written directly in world space — and then owns their disposal itself, since
+nothing will cascade for it. (The live counterweight: `TileGridBakeSystem` still

+and a baked-collider producer is exactly the code that can turn thousands of entities into

+parent to be found by detection (the auto-`ColliderTagComponent` is what detection queries)
+and no parent to resolve its body (it resolves to itself).

+a per-frame dictionary rebuild, showing up as a flat frame-time tax that profiles inside
+`HierarchySystem` and looks nothing like a collision problem. Unparenting them without moving
+the disposal responsibility to the producer leaks every collider the producer forgets — there

Per the maintainer's decision on #35, tooling ships as **documented recipes, not CLI commands** — each page states the problem, the traps, and points at `roo-oliv/gmtk-2026gj` → `tools/` as the reference implementation to copy and adapt (with an explicit "Adapt these" list).

Done — commit `6cc18a0` is on PR #79 and the PR body now reflects it.

**The fix**, in both sites the premise flagged:

- **`ButtonMeshPrepSystem`** — its update path mutated the existing `DrawComponent` in place, including `Target`, which feeds `MasterRenderSystem`'s value-predicate draw sets (built once, re-evaluated only on publication). It now snapshots whether the target actually changed before the rewrite and calls `entity.NotifyChanged<DrawComponent>()` only on a real retarget — deliberately not unconditionally, because the system runs per button per frame and the premise's own warning is that a per-frame notify re-runs every pass's predicate every frame.
- **`HudPreviewSystem`** — both mutation sites now publish the `DynamicTextComponent` flip: the HUD→Main projection notifies guarded on the actual retarget (it runs every Edit frame), and `Restore` notifies unconditionally since it only runs on the transition back. Previously only `TransformComponent` was notified, and the code was safe purely because `TextPrepSystem` happens to rebuild the `DrawComponent` via `Set` the same frame.

Neither notify fires under any shipping code path today (no code currently changes those targets after creation), so this is a pure gap-closure with no behavior change — exactly the "one requirement-change away" risk the new foundation premise documents.

**Verification:** full-solution `dotnet test MonoDreams.sln --configuration Release` passed — 1254 engine tests + 57 CLI tests, 0 failures (confirmed via the `Aprovado!` lines, not just the exit code). The `packages.lock.json` churn from restore was reverted before committing, so the PR stays clean.
